questions.stem: Why does doubling the concentration roughly double the collision count?

options.text: Because collisions per second are proportional to the number of particles present
options.explanation: Twice the particles in the same volume meet twice as often.

options.text: Because each particle then moves faster
options.explanation: Concentration changes crowding, not particle speed.

options.text: Because the volume doubles too
options.explanation: The volume stays the same; the population doubles.

options.text: Because the acid becomes stronger chemically
options.explanation: The explanation is mechanical crowding, not chemical strength.

questions.stem: How does increased pressure speed up a gaseous reaction?

options.text: The same number of particles is forced into a smaller volume, so collisions become more frequent
options.explanation: Squeezing the crowd raises the bump rate per second.

options.text: Pressure adds energy to each particle
options.explanation: Pressure changes spacing; energy belongs to the temperature story.

options.text: Pressure creates extra particles
options.explanation: The particle count is unchanged.

options.text: Pressure only affects liquids
options.explanation: Pressure effects are quoted for gases in this topic.

questions.stem: What converts an ordinary collision into a successful one?

options.text: Enough energy and the right arrangement, so product molecules form
options.explanation: Only a proportion of collisions carry what it takes to react.

options.text: The particles colliding head-on at any speed
options.explanation: Direction alone is not enough without the energy requirement.

options.text: The particles sticking together permanently
options.explanation: Products form and separate; permanent sticking is not the rule.

options.text: The presence of a catalyst in every collision
options.explanation: Catalysts are absent in most explained reactions here.

questions.stem: A flask of gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to the rate?

options.text: It increases because the particle crowding and collision count rise
options.explanation: Half the volume means twice the crowding, so collisions per second rise.

options.text: It decreases because particles have less room to move
options.explanation: Less room means more meetings, not fewer.

options.text: It stays the same because particle count is fixed
options.explanation: Count is fixed but crowding is not.

options.text: It doubles only if a catalyst is added
options.explanation: No catalyst is needed for the pressure effect.

questions.stem: Which chain of reasoning correctly explains a faster rate at higher concentration?

options.text: More particles per volume, more collisions per second, more successful collisions, faster rate
options.explanation: Each link follows from the previous one and ends at the rate.

options.text: Faster rate, more collisions, more particles, higher concentration
options.explanation: The chain runs backwards from the outcome.

options.text: Higher concentration, slower particles, fewer collisions, faster rate
options.explanation: Speed and count are mixed up mid-chain.

options.text: More particles, fewer collisions, faster rate
options.explanation: The middle link contradicts crowding.

questions.stem: Why does a 10 °C rise have such a large effect on rate?

options.text: Because collisions become both more frequent and more energetic
options.explanation: The two effects combine, with the energy gain doing the greater work.

options.text: Because particles double in size
options.explanation: Particle size does not change with temperature.

options.text: Because the concentration rises with temperature
options.explanation: Concentration is a separate factor.

options.text: Because the reaction switches to a faster pathway
options.explanation: No new pathway appears; the same one runs faster.

questions.stem: What does the rough rule of thumb state for aqueous and gaseous systems?

options.text: Every 10 °C increase in temperature approximately doubles the rate
options.explanation: The stated rule of thumb links a 10 °C step to a doubling of rate.

options.text: Every 10 °C increase halves the rate
options.explanation: Heating speeds reactions; the rule says doubles.

options.text: Every 1 °C increase doubles the rate
options.explanation: The doubling belongs to a 10 °C step.

options.text: Rate is unaffected below 50 °C
options.explanation: No threshold appears in the rule.

questions.stem: Why does powdering a solid reactant speed up the reaction?

options.text: More solid particles are exposed to the other reactant, so collisions per second increase
options.explanation: Exposure is the whole story; the powder meets the solution everywhere at once.

options.text: Powder particles move faster than lumps
options.explanation: Speed of particles is a temperature effect, not a surface effect.

options.text: Powdering raises the concentration of the solution
options.explanation: The solid is not part of the solution concentration.

options.text: Powder lowers the activation energy
options.explanation: Only catalysts lower the energy barrier.

questions.stem: A student claims doubling the surface area doubles the amount of product formed. What is the correction?

options.text: Doubling the surface area doubles the collision count, not the final product amount
options.explanation: The plateau is fixed by the starting quantities; only the pace changes.

options.text: The claim is correct because rate and yield are identical
options.explanation: Rate and yield are different quantities.

options.text: Doubling the surface area halves the product
options.explanation: No such penalty exists.

options.text: Product amount depends on the powder colour
options.explanation: Colour is irrelevant to yield.

questions.stem: Which factor affects reaction rate by increasing both the number and the energy of collisions?

options.text: Temperature
options.explanation: Heat raises particle speed, so collisions come more often and hit harder.

options.text: Surface area
options.explanation: Surface area changes only the number of exposed collision sites.

options.text: Concentration
options.explanation: Concentration changes crowding, not particle energy.

options.text: A catalyst
options.explanation: A catalyst changes the energy barrier, not the particle energies.
